newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S.Commerce Secy promises Americas free trade push.
newsitem.headline: U.S.Commerce Secy promises Americas free trade push.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley issued a spirited defence of the embattled North American Free Trade Agreement on Wednesday and pledged to work to expand the pact throughout the Americas.

During part of a visit with U.S. President Bill Clinton to the United States' third-largest trading partner, Daley said NAFTA had helped create jobs in the United States since the pact took effect in 1994.
"I'd like to get the record straight: NAFTA is working," the former Chicago businessman told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Mexico City, the largest of its kind in the world.

Daley said the Clinton administration planned to work with business in spreading the free-trade gospel and convincing sceptics that NAFTA has created jobs rather than allowing them to leak to Mexico, as some had feared.
"NAFTA has been a job creator, not a job drain," he said, adding that exports to Canada and Mexico now support some three million U.S. jobs, 300,000 of which have been created since the pact began.
U.S. exports to Mexico and Canada have grown 80 percent since NAFTA took effect and now outstrip total U.S. exports to either the Pacific Rim or Europe, Daley said.
Mexico could soon replace Japan as the United States' second-largest trading partner, according to U.S. officials.

Critics of the NAFTA accord have pointed to a U.S. trade deficit with Mexico as evidence the deal is sour, and U.S. labour and environmental groups on Monday urged Clinton to fix the agreement during his Mexico visit, saying 420,000 jobs had been lost because of the pact.
Daley said U.S. exports to Mexico are growing at about 21 percent, outstripping the growth of imports from Mexico.
"The growth rate of U.S. exports to both (Mexico and Canada) is outpacing our imports, which will hopefully take some of the political pressure off the sensitive trade imbalance," he said.

The next logical step, Daley said, was to push for a hemisphere-wide free-trade agreement by 2005. To do so, he said the Clinton administration would work closely with Congress in the next few months to regain the so-called "fast track" authority allowing it to negotiate trade pacts and win only final Congressional approval.

"Our primary challenge is to keep the momentum for liberalisation and privatisation going. Regrettably, the loss of fast-track provides confidence to those in the region who favour a go-slow approach or would seek to weaken the (region-wide agreement)," he said.
The United States will try to convince South American nations to begin negotiations on a free trade pact during the second Summit of the Americas in Chile next year, Daley said.
But the nations of the Mercosur free-trade agreement -- Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay -- want to slow hemishpere-wide free-trade, Daley said.
"Mercosur prefers to go slowly, but market access negotiations involving 34 countries ... will be a long and complicated process. We need to get moving fast," he said.
